key: writing an amount on a cheque only
name: ch04_cheque_figures_and_words
alt: A cheque with a very long amount written only in figures is misread by a clerk with a small calculator, while a second cheque also carries the amount in words.
scene: A split-panel illustration divided by a thin vertical line, set at a bank counter with a wooden top and a steel grille. LEFT panel: a large cheque lies on the counter with a very long amount written only in figures in the amount box and the words line left completely blank. A tired bank clerk in his 50s with spectacles, a sleeveless sweater and a pen behind his ear copies the amount into a small pocket calculator whose narrow display has room for fewer digits, so the last digit on the display comes out different from the cheque; a tiny magnifier inset shows the final digit 3 on the cheque turning into a 2 on the calculator. The clerk looks calm and unaware, and an orange question-mark badge floats near the calculator to show nobody noticed. RIGHT panel: the same kind of cheque, but now the amount is written twice, once in figures and once on the words line as a long handwritten line, drawn as wavy ink. A young customer in a blue kurta points at the words line, and a green tick sits beside it, showing the words copy is the safe one to use. A small note on the right reminds that someone must actually read the words line rather than the figures. Bright, neutral bank-hall light, a clock and a token display on the back wall. Labels: "FIGURES ONLY" above the left panel, "IN WORDS TOO" above the right panel.

key: school register where every single page
name: ch04_register_headings_once
alt: Two school registers: one repeats the column headings on every page, the other prints them once on the cover and the pages hold only values.
scene: A classroom teacher's desk seen from slightly above, with two attendance-and-marks registers lying open side by side and a thin vertical line dividing the picture. LEFT half: a thick register fanned open so that several pages are visible, and on every single page the same bold heading row with three columns, roll number, name and marks, is written out again at the top in heavy ink, so the headings take up a big share of each page; a schoolteacher in her 40s in a green cotton sari and spectacles sighs as she writes the heading row once more on a fresh page, her pen hand tired, while the pages pile up thick. RIGHT half: a slimmer register whose cover is turned back to show the heading row printed only once, neatly, on the inside cover; the pages after it hold only compact rows of values, small numbers and short names, with no headings at all, so the book is visibly thinner. A small dotted arrow runs from one value row back to the heading on the cover, showing where its meaning lives. In the top corner of the right half, a small inset shows a loose page being posted alone in an envelope, with a question mark asking how the reader gets the cover. Chalkboard and a globe in the background, morning classroom light. Labels: "HEADINGS EVERY PAGE" above the left register, "SCHEMA ONCE" above the right register's cover.

key: change your name spelling on the card
name: ch04_aadhaar_field_tags
alt: An identity card keeps the same number after a name-spelling change, but a reused number makes an old file point at a stranger.
scene: A split-panel illustration divided by a thin vertical line, inside a government records office with tall steel cupboards and paper files. LEFT panel: a young man in a striped shirt holds up two versions of his plastic identity card, the old card with his name spelled one way and the new card with a corrected spelling, while a large twelve-digit-style number band, drawn as a row of grey blocks, stays identical on both cards and is linked by a straight green line to three office counters, a bank, a gas agency and a mobile shop, each with a green tick showing they still find him. RIGHT panel: a careless office clerk in a grey shirt peels the same number band off an old card and sticks it onto a brand-new card belonging to an elderly woman in a purple sari, while an old file folder on the desk, still pointing to that number with a dashed arrow, now opens to show her photo instead of the young man's; a red cross and a warning triangle hover above the file, and nobody in the office notices the swap. The mood on the left is relieved and orderly; on the right it is quiet and wrong, not dramatic. Fluorescent tube lights, stacks of forms, a wall clock. Labels: "RENAME OK" above the left panel, "NEVER REUSE" above the right panel.

key: The tin carries only a few painted marks
name: ch04_dabbawala_shared_code
alt: A dabbawala reads a few painted marks on a lunch tin because he knows the shared code, while a stranger sees only meaningless paint.
scene: A railway platform in Mumbai in the late morning, with a long wooden crate full of round steel lunch tins in cloth bags. The hero is one tin held up close: its lid carries only a few short painted marks, a coloured dot, a small letter and a two-digit number, arranged in three tidy columns. LEFT side: a lean dabbawala in a white kurta-pyjama and a white Gandhi cap glances at the lid and knows instantly where it goes; a thought bubble above his head shows the meaning of each column as small icons, a train for the station column, a building for the office column and a desk for the floor column, with dotted lines from each painted mark to its icon. RIGHT side: a puzzled tourist in a sun hat and backpack holds an identical tin and stares at the same marks, and his thought bubble shows only blobs of paint and a big question mark. In the background a second dabbawala loads tins onto a bicycle with a long carrier, and a local train waits at the platform. The idea is that the marks are tiny because the meaning lives in the readers' heads, the shared code. Hazy morning light, busy but orderly mood. Labels: "MARKS" on a small tag next to the tin lid, "SCHEMA" above the dabbawala's thought bubble.

name: ch04_society_notices_group
alt: Several residents post a text, a photo and a PDF into one society chat group that delivers each item to every member's phone, and one member forwards a notice whole.
scene: A housing-society scene drawn as one big flow from left to right. LEFT: three residents posting from their balconies or the lobby: a society secretary in his 60s in a white kurta posting a short text bubble, a young mother in a salwar suit posting a small photo of a water tank, and a security supervisor in a blue uniform posting a document icon with a folded corner. Each post flies as a sealed envelope into the CENTRE, where a large round chat-group hub shaped like a notice board sits on a pillar, with the three envelopes dropping in unopened, because the group does not care what is inside. RIGHT: from the hub, copies of every envelope fly out to a column of five phones held by different members, a student, an old man, a cook, a woman with shopping bags and a teenager. At the bottom right, one member forwards a notice to another group: she passes the whole sealed envelope along with a green tick, while beside her a faded ghost of a torn half-envelope with a red cross shows the wrong way, retyping only the part understood. Bright afternoon light on a residential tower, potted plants on the balconies. Labels: "PRODUCERS" over the posting residents, "SUBSCRIBERS" over the column of phones, "FORWARD WHOLE" by the forwarding member.
